key_terms.meaning: A table of upshift and downshift vehicle speeds, each held against throttle opening, that tells the transmission when to change gear.
The controller that reads throttle, vehicle speed and turbine speed, picks a gear from the shift map and drives the shift solenoids.
A forced downshift when the accelerator is pressed past a set point; the operating point jumps left of the downshift line on the shift map.
The speed v<sub>set</sub> the driver stores with the cruise button; the closed loop works to keep v ≈ v<sub>set</sub>.
t<sub>gap</sub> = d ÷ v, where d is the gap to the car ahead in m and v is the host speed in m/s; ACC holds it at the selected t<sub>target</sub>, often 1.5 to 2.5 s.
v − v<sub>lead</sub>, the speed at which the gap to the car ahead shrinks, in m/s; positive when closing.
A calibrated twist bar between the steering column and the pinion; the angle it twists through measures the driver's steering torque.
A lookup giving motor current (or assist torque) against measured steering torque and vehicle speed; assist torque at the pinion T<sub>assist</sub> = N × k<sub>t</sub> × I<sub>m</sub>.
An electric power steering layout with the motor on the steering column inside the cabin, common on small cars.
An electric power steering layout with the motor and reduction drive on the steering rack, used on heavier cars.
An EPS function that adds torque towards straight ahead at low speed when the driver's torque falls away.
λ = (v − ωr) / v, where v is vehicle speed in m/s, ω is wheel angular speed in rad/s and r is wheel radius in m; peak grip sits near λ = 0.1 to 0.2.
The ABS build–hold–release sequence of the inlet and outlet valves, repeated many times a second at each wheel.
r, the rate at which the car rotates about its vertical axis, in rad/s or degrees per second.
r<sub>des</sub> = vδ ÷ (L + Kv²), the yaw rate the driver's steering angle and speed ask for, from a bicycle model, capped at μg ÷ v by the friction the road can give.
M<sub>z</sub> = F<sub>x</sub> × (t ÷ 2), the turning moment about the vertical axis from a brake force F<sub>x</sub> at one wheel, t ÷ 2 being half the track width in m.
A control law that asks the actuator to damp the body against an imaginary fixed point in the sky while leaving wheel motion free.
F = −c<sub>sky</sub> × v<sub>body</sub>; a semi-active damper can give it only when F × v<sub>rel</sub> < 0.
The small electric detonator that fires the gas generator of an airbag when the crash sensor commands deployment.
Average deceleration a = v² ÷ (2s) over crush distance s, lasting t = 2s ÷ v.
TTC = d / v<sub>rel</sub>, where d is the gap in m and v<sub>rel</sub> the closing speed in m/s; a warning or brake request is issued below a threshold.
Combining radar, camera and other measurements into one consistent list of objects around the car.
s = v t<sub>d</sub> + v² ÷ (2a): delay distance plus braking distance.
K<sub>p</sub>, the multiplier on the speed error e = v<sub>ref</sub> − v; it sets how hard the force (or throttle) answers an error.
K<sub>i</sub>, the multiplier on the integral of the speed error; it removes the steady-state speed error left by K<sub>p</sub> alone.
T<sub>i</sub> = τ and K<sub>p</sub> = τ ÷ (Kλ) for a plant K ÷ (τs + 1); the closed loop becomes 1 ÷ (λs + 1).

takeaways: A TCU chooses the shift point from a map and then shapes clutch pressure, so shift quality is a hydraulic control problem.
Cruise control is one closed loop on throttle; adaptive cruise control adds a second loop on gap that may also use the brakes.
Electric power steering replaces hydraulic pressure with motor current, and the assist map is the heart of its design.
ABS holds wheel slip near the peak of the friction curve by cycling brake pressure; traction control does the same job with drive torque.
ESP compares the yaw rate the driver asked for with the yaw rate the car has, then brakes one wheel to correct the difference.
An active suspension drives a force actuator at each corner so the body stays flat while the wheels follow the road.
An airbag is a supplement to the seat belt, fired by a crash sensor within milliseconds of a severe impact.
ADAS is a stack: sense, fuse, plan, act, at a defined level of automation.
PI control removes steady-state speed error, PD control adds damping, and two gains plus a plant model are all a speed loop needs.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on the control loop drawn correctly, the sensors and actuators named, and the reason for each action given, not on the list of parts alone.

bank.q: Explain the working of an electronic transmission control system. Cover the inputs to the TCU, how the shift map fixes the shift point, and how clutch pressure is controlled during the shift itself.
outline: Inputs: throttle position, vehicle speed, engine speed, turbine speed, oil temperature
Shift map: upshift and downshift lines plotted against throttle opening; hysteresis stops hunting
Shift decision: compare present gear and speed with the map; check the shift is safe for engine speed
During the shift: reduce engine torque (retard or throttle), ramp clutch pressure through the torque phase and the inertia phase
End of shift: on-coming clutch to full line pressure, torque reduction ended, shift time measured and the adaptive correction stored
answer: The system is a closed loop: sensors feed the transmission control unit (TCU); the TCU picks a gear from its shift map and drives solenoid valves; the valves set the oil pressure on the clutch pistons; the clutches change the ratio; shaft speed sensors report back how the shift went.

answer.text: Inputs and what each one is used for:

head: Input
Sensor or source
Used for
rows: driver demand: the vertical axis of the shift map, kickdown
output shaft or wheel speed sensor
the horizontal axis of the shift map
engine speed limits after the shift, torque estimate
measures slip and the real shift time
fill time and pressure correction, cold and hot modes

answer: Shift map: for each pair of gears there is an upshift line and a downshift line on a graph of throttle opening against vehicle speed. Right of the upshift line the higher gear is chosen; left of the downshift line the lower gear. The two lines are kept apart (hysteresis), so at a steady speed on one line the box does not hunt between two gears. Light throttle moves the shift points to low speed for economy; heavy throttle moves them up so the engine stays near its power range.

Example of a shift decision: a car at 60 km/h and 30 % throttle is in top gear (ratio 0.70, final drive 3.50, wheel radius 0.30 m). The wheel turns at (16.67 ÷ 1.885) × 60 = 530.5 rpm, so the engine turns at 530.5 × 3.50 × 0.70 = 1300 rpm. The driver presses to 90 %: that point lies left of the downshift line, so the TCU selects the direct gear (1.00) and the engine goes to 530.5 × 3.50 = 1857 rpm.

Before it shifts, the TCU checks that the engine speed after the shift stays inside its limits: a downshift that would push the engine past its red line is refused, and an upshift that would drop it below a lugging limit is delayed.

answer.text: Pressure control during the shift, phase by phase:

head: Phase
What the TCU does
What goes wrong if it is mistimed
rows: short high-pressure pulse fills the on-coming piston until the plates touch
too short: the clutch is late and the engine flares
on-coming pressure ramps up while the off-going clutch is released
release too early: flare; overlap too long: tie-up and a jerk
engine speed moves to the new ratio; the TCU asks for a short torque cut (spark retard)
no torque cut: a step felt by the passengers
on-coming clutch to full line pressure, torque cut ended
low pressure: the clutch slips and burns

answer: Line pressure follows engine torque because a clutch carries torque T = μ × p × A × r<sub>m</sub> × n, with μ the friction coefficient, p the oil pressure, A the piston area, r<sub>m</sub> the mean friction radius and n the number of friction faces. For example μ = 0.12, A = 0.006 m², r<sub>m</sub> = 0.06 m and n = 6 give 0.12 × 0.006 × 0.06 × 6 = 0.000259 N·m per pascal, so 5 bar (5 × 10⁵ Pa) carries 130 N·m. Double the torque needs double the pressure, so the variable-force solenoid raises line pressure with throttle.

Adaptive learning: the turbine and output speed sensors time each shift. If the engine flared, the next fill pulse is made longer or the pressure higher; if the shift was harsh, the opposite. The corrections are stored per gear pair and oil temperature, so the box keeps its shift quality as the clutches wear.

Check: the speed relation n<sub>engine</sub> = n<sub>wheel</sub> × i<sub>gear</sub> × i<sub>final</sub> gives 1300 rpm and 1857 rpm, a 557 rpm rise, which the TCU must cover in the inertia phase; and the clutch formula shows pressure in proportion to torque.

bank.q: Describe cruise control and adaptive cruise control. Draw the loops and state exactly what each loop controls and what each one can actuate.
outline: Cruise control: error e = v<sub>set</sub> − v, PI controller, electronic throttle, no brake authority
ACC: outer gap loop produces a speed demand, which the inner speed loop follows
Modes: speed control, gap control, follow, and cut-in handling
Actuators: throttle, gearbox, and the brake system for ACC
Safety: driver override on brake or clutch, minimum gap, sensor loss fallback
answer: Cruise control is one loop. The driver presses SET above a minimum speed and the controller stores v<sub>set</sub>. The error e = v<sub>set</sub> − v, with v from the wheel speed sensors, drives a PI controller: u = K<sub>p</sub>e + K<sub>i</sub>∫e dt. The output u is a throttle command, 0 to 100 %, sent to the electronic throttle.

answer.text: Loop sketch of basic cruise control, in words:
answer.pre:
v<sub>set</sub> ──►(Σ)──e──► PI ──u──► electronic throttle ──► engine and car ──► v
           ▲−                                                     │
           └──────────────── wheel speed sensors ◄────────────────┘

answer: What basic cruise controls and can actuate: it controls speed only, and its only actuator is the throttle (with the gearbox following its own map). The integral term removes the speed error on a hill. It has no brake authority, so on a long downhill the car can run above v<sub>set</sub>; closing the throttle is all it can do.

Adaptive cruise control (ACC) adds a forward radar (about 77 GHz) or a camera, and an outer gap loop. The radar measures the distance d to the in-path car and the relative speed. The driver picks a time gap t<sub>target</sub>, often 1.5 to 2.5 s, so the wanted distance d<sub>target</sub> = t<sub>target</sub> × v grows with speed.

answer.pre:
outer gap loop:  e<sub>gap</sub> = d − t<sub>target</sub> × v  ──►  speed demand v<sub>dem</sub>  (never above v<sub>set</sub>)
inner speed loop: v<sub>dem</sub> − v  ──► PI ──► throttle, or a brake request to the ESP unit

answer: Modes: speed control when the lane ahead is clear (v<sub>dem</sub> = v<sub>set</sub>); gap control when a slower car is ahead; follow mode, matching its speed at the target gap; and cut-in handling, when d drops suddenly and the controller brakes hard or warns the driver to brake.

Worked numbers: host set to 25 m/s, lead car at 20 m/s and 60 m, 2.0 s gap. Time gap 60 ÷ 25 = 2.4 s; target 2.0 × 25 = 50 m; gap error +10 m; closing rate 5 m/s; TTC 60 ÷ 5 = 12 s. A steady relative deceleration of 5² ÷ (2 × 10) = 1.25 m/s² for 4 s brings the host to 20 m/s exactly at 50 m.

answer.text: What each loop controls and actuates:

head: Cruise control
Adaptive cruise control
rows: wheel speeds, radar, camera, yaw rate
throttle, gearbox downshift, service brakes through ESP
brakes, up to a comfort limit

answer: Safety: the brake pedal always cancels; the accelerator overrides; there is a minimum selectable gap; ACC brake demand is limited (comfort systems often a few m/s²), so a close cut-in hands back to the driver with a warning; if the radar is blocked or faulty ACC switches off with a message and normal cruise is not silently kept on.
Check: 2.0 s at 25 m/s is 50 m and at 20 m/s is 40 m, so the target distance shrinks as the host slows, which is why time gap, not distance, is the setting.

Torsion bar twists with driver torque; twist angle is measured optically or magnetically
Steering angle sensor gives absolute wheel angle for return-to-centre and for ESP
Motor current set from the assist map against torque and speed
Fail-safe: motor off, manual steering must remain

answer: Parts: steering wheel, upper column, torsion bar with a torque sensor, steering angle sensor, brushless or brushed DC motor, worm and worm-wheel reduction on the column, ECU, lower column with universal joints, pinion and rack. The motor sits inside the cabin, which keeps it dry and cool; this suits small and medium cars.

Torsion bar: a thin shaft joins the upper column (driver side) to the lower column (pinion side). When the driver turns against the tyres the bar twists by a small angle in proportion to torque. A Hall-effect or inductive sensor measures the relative angle of its two ends without contact. For example, a bar of 2 N·m per degree twists 2° when the driver applies 4 N·m. Zero twist means no driver torque, so the ECU gives no assist.

Steering angle sensor: it measures the steering-wheel angle over several turns lock to lock, using geared magnets with Hall sensors or an optical code disc. The ECU uses it for return-to-centre and for damping; the ESP uses it, divided by the steering ratio, for the road-wheel angle in its yaw reference.

Assist: the ECU reads driver torque and vehicle speed, looks up the assist map and sets motor current. The assist at the pinion is T<sub>assist</sub> = N × k<sub>t</sub> × I<sub>m</sub>. With N = 16, k<sub>t</sub> = 0.05 N·m/A: parking assist of 40 N·m needs 40 ÷ 16 = 2.5 N·m of motor torque and 2.5 ÷ 0.05 = 50 A; highway assist of 4 N·m needs 0.25 N·m and 5 A. With the driver's 4 N·m the pinion gets 44 N·m, a rack force of 44 ÷ 0.008 = 5.5 kN.

Fail-safe: torque and angle signals are checked against each other and for range. On a fault the ECU ramps the assist down and a relay or clutch disconnects the motor; the column, worm wheel and rack still connect the wheel to the road, so the driver steers manually with more effort and a warning lamp lights.
Check: the assist falls from 40 to 4 N·m between parking and 120 km/h, a factor of ten, and the current falls from 50 A to 5 A with it, as T<sub>assist</sub> = N k<sub>t</sub> I<sub>m</sub> requires.

bank.q: Explain the build, hold and release phases of an ABS pressure cycle, and say why slip is held near the peak of the friction curve.
outline: Wheel speed sensors give ω; vehicle speed estimated from the four wheels
Slip λ = (v − ωr)/v; friction curve has a peak near λ = 0.1 to 0.2
Build: inlet valve open, outlet valve closed, pressure rises
Hold: both valves closed, pressure held
Release: inlet closed, outlet open, fluid to the accumulator, pump returns it
Cycle rate of about 5 to 15 per second; why locked wheel gives less grip and no steering
answer: Sensing: a toothed ring and a speed sensor at each wheel give ω. The ABS unit estimates vehicle speed v from the four wheels (the fastest wheel during braking, corrected with the deceleration it expects), and finds the slip of each wheel.

Slip ratio: λ = (v − ωr) ÷ v, where r is the rolling radius. λ = 0 is free rolling and λ = 1 is a locked wheel. The friction coefficient μ rises with slip to a peak near λ = 0.15 to 0.2 on dry asphalt (a little lower on wet) and then falls towards the locked value.

Hardware per wheel: an inlet valve (normally open) between the master cylinder and the brake, an outlet valve (normally closed) from the brake to a low-pressure accumulator, and a return pump that sends the fluid back to the master cylinder side.

answer.text: Example at v = 20 m/s, r = 0.30 m and a target band 0.10 ≤ λ ≤ 0.20:

answer: The cycle: as pressure builds the wheel decelerates and λ rises; when λ passes the band (or the wheel deceleration passes a threshold) the ECU holds, then releases; the wheel speeds up again, λ falls, and the ECU holds and builds again. This repeats about 5 to 15 times a second at each wheel, which the driver feels as pedal pulsing.

Why the peak: the braking force is μ × the wheel load, so holding λ near the peak gives the most force: in the example 1.17 against 0.76 locked, about 54 % more. A rolling tyre also keeps its side force, so the driver can still steer round an obstacle; a locked tyre slides in the direction the car is moving and the steering does nothing.
Limits: on loose gravel or fresh snow a locked wheel can build a wedge of material in front of it and stop sooner, so ABS may lengthen the stop there; the gain is steering control.
Check: every λ in the table comes from (20 − ωr) ÷ 20, and the action follows its position against the band: below build, inside hold, above release.

bank.q: Explain the electronic stability program. How does it decide that the car is understeering or oversteering, and what does it do about each?
outline: Inputs: steering angle, yaw rate, lateral acceleration, wheel speeds, brake pressure
Reference yaw rate from the bicycle model, limited by the friction available
Error = reference yaw rate − measured yaw rate
Oversteer: brake the outer front wheel; understeer: brake the inner rear wheel
Also cut engine torque and raise brake pressure at the chosen wheel only
Worked at the level of a yaw moment M<sub>z</sub> = F<sub>x</sub> × (t ÷ 2)
answer: Purpose: ESP keeps the car turning the way the driver steers when the tyres start to slide sideways. It compares the yaw rate the driver asks for with the yaw rate the car has and brakes one wheel to correct the difference, and it cuts engine torque if drive force feeds the slide.

Inputs: steering angle sensor (steering-wheel angle, divided by the steering ratio to give δ); yaw rate sensor (a MEMS gyro); lateral acceleration sensor; four wheel speed sensors (vehicle speed and slip); brake pressure sensor; engine torque over CAN.

Reference yaw rate from the bicycle model: r<sub>des</sub> = vδ ÷ (L + Kv²), with v in m/s, δ in rad, wheelbase L in m and understeer term K in s²/m. It is capped by grip: lateral acceleration v × r cannot exceed μg, so r<sub>des</sub> ≤ μg ÷ v.

Numbers: L = 2.6 m, K = 0.0025 s²/m, v = 20 m/s, δ = 0.05 rad. Kv² = 1.0 m, so r<sub>des</sub> = 1.0 ÷ 3.6 = 0.278 rad/s (15.9 °/s). The cap for μ = 0.9 is 0.9 × 9.81 ÷ 20 = 0.441 rad/s, so the reference stands.

Decision: with yaw counted positive in the direction of the turn, e = r<sub>des</sub> − r<sub>meas</sub>. A positive error (the car turns less than asked) is understeer; a negative error (it turns more) is oversteer. If the sensor reads 0.200 rad/s, e = +0.078 rad/s: understeer. The lateral accelerometer confirms: v × r<sub>meas</sub> = 20 × 0.2 = 4 m/s² is well inside the grip.

answer.text: What ESP does in each case:

answer: Size of the correction: a brake force F<sub>x</sub> at one wheel, at half the track width t ÷ 2 from the centre line, gives a yaw moment M<sub>z</sub> = F<sub>x</sub> × (t ÷ 2). With 2000 N at the left rear wheel of a 1.5 m track, M<sub>z</sub> = 2000 × 0.75 = 1500 N·m into the turn. The hydraulic unit raises pressure at that one wheel only; the other wheels are held.
Engine torque: ESP also asks the engine or motor controller to cut torque, because a driven tyre that is also pushing has less grip left for cornering.
Limits: ESP works only within the friction the road gives; on ice it cannot make the car turn more sharply than the tyres allow, and switching it off adds no grip.

Check: the understeer case gives a positive error and a moment into the turn, which raises r<sub>meas</sub> towards 0.278 rad/s; braking the front outer wheel in this case would make the understeer worse.

bank.q: A car travels at v = 20 m/s and a braked wheel has rim speed ωr = 15 m/s. Compute the slip ratio and state what the ABS does next at that wheel.
outline: Compare with the peak near 0.1 to 0.2, so the wheel is past the peak
ABS releases pressure at that wheel
Once λ falls back, hold, then build again
Torque and steering behaviour at high slip
answer: Data: vehicle speed v = 20 m/s, rim (tread) speed ωr = 15 m/s.

Position on the friction curve: the peak is near λ = 0.15 to 0.2 (about 0.17 on dry asphalt), and the ABS target band is about 0.10 to 0.20. λ = 0.25 is past the peak, on the falling side, where a small rise in brake torque makes the wheel slow down faster and run towards lock.

Friction at this slip on the dry curve of the chapter, μ = 1.2801(1 − e<sup>−23.99λ</sup>) − 0.52λ: μ(0.25) = 1.2801 × 0.9975 − 0.130 = 1.15, just below the peak of 1.17 but falling; at lock it would be 0.76.

ABS action now: release. The inlet valve closes and the outlet valve opens, so fluid flows to the low-pressure accumulator and the return pump runs. Brake torque falls, the road drives the wheel back up to speed and λ falls.
Target for the recovery: for λ = 0.15 the rim speed must return to ωr = (1 − 0.15) × 20 = 17 m/s; the band 0.10 to 0.20 is a rim speed of 16 to 18 m/s.

Next steps: when the wheel is back in the band the ECU holds (both valves closed); as the wheel steadies it builds again (inlet open, outlet closed) in small steps, and the cycle repeats 5 to 15 times a second while the driver keeps the pedal down.

Behaviour at high slip: past the peak the longitudinal force falls a little but the side force falls a lot, so the car loses steering; that, more than the small loss of braking force, is why the ECU acts at once.
Check: 0.25 > 0.20, so release is right; λ = 0.25 means the tread is 25 % slower than the car, and 20 × (1 − 0.25) = 15 m/s matches the given rim speed.

bank.q: Explain how PI gains are selected for a vehicle speed control loop. Take a first-order plant G(s) = K/(τs + 1) and show how K<sub>p</sub> and K<sub>i</sub> set the closed-loop response.
outline: Error e = v<sub>set</sub> − v; u = K<sub>p</sub> e + K<sub>i</sub> ∫e dt
Closed-loop second-order form with ω<sub>n</sub> and ζ written in terms of K<sub>p</sub>, K<sub>i</sub>, K and τ
Choose ζ near 0.7 and ω<sub>n</sub> for the rise time, or cancel the plant pole (T<sub>i</sub> = τ, lambda tuning) for a first-order loop
K<sub>i</sub> removes the steady-state error that resistance and road grade would leave with K<sub>p</sub> alone
Saturation, anti-windup, derivative filtering and rate limits
Road grade as a disturbance the integrator must absorb
answer: Plant: m dv/dt = F − bv, so V(s) ÷ F(s) = K ÷ (τs + 1) with K = 1/b and τ = m/b. For m = 1500 kg and b = 100 N/(m/s): K = 0.01 (m/s)/N and τ = 15 s.
Controller: e = v<sub>ref</sub> − v and F = K<sub>p</sub>e + K<sub>i</sub>∫e dt, with K<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/T<sub>i</sub>. In Laplace form C(s) = K<sub>p</sub> + K<sub>i</sub>/s.

answer.pre:
V/V<sub>ref</sub> = C G ÷ (1 + C G) = K(K<sub>p</sub> s + K<sub>i</sub>) ÷ [τ s² + (1 + K K<sub>p</sub>) s + K K<sub>i</sub>]
compare with s² + 2ζω<sub>n</sub> s + ω<sub>n</sub>²:
ω<sub>n</sub>² = K K<sub>i</sub> ÷ τ        2ζω<sub>n</sub> = (1 + K K<sub>p</sub>) ÷ τ

answer: Method 1, pole placement: choose ζ near 0.7 for a small overshoot and ω<sub>n</sub> for the rise time. For ζ = 0.7 and ω<sub>n</sub> = 0.5 rad/s: K<sub>i</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>²τ ÷ K = 0.25 × 15 ÷ 0.01 = 375 N/m and K<sub>p</sub> = (2ζω<sub>n</sub>τ − 1) ÷ K = (10.5 − 1) ÷ 0.01 = 950 N/(m/s). The PI zero at −K<sub>i</sub>/K<sub>p</sub> = −0.39 rad/s adds some overshoot beyond the 4.6 % that ζ = 0.7 alone gives, so check the step response.

Method 2, lambda tuning: set T<sub>i</sub> = τ so the PI zero cancels the plant pole, and K<sub>p</sub> = τ ÷ (Kλ). Then the loop gain is 1/(λs) and the closed loop is 1/(λs + 1), first order with no overshoot. For λ = 3 s: K<sub>p</sub> = 15 ÷ (0.01 × 3) = 500 N/(m/s), T<sub>i</sub> = 15 s, K<sub>i</sub> = 33.3 N/m.

Check of method 2 with the formulas above: τs² + (1 + 5)s + 0.333 = 15s² + 6s + 0.333 = 0 has roots −1/15 and −1/3 rad/s. The root −1/15 is cancelled by the PI zero at −33.3/500 = −1/15, and the root −1/3 is the wanted 1/λ.

Steady-state error: without integral action the speed settles where K<sub>p</sub>(v<sub>ref</sub> − v) = bv; for K<sub>p</sub> = 500 and v<sub>ref</sub> = 30 m/s, v = 25 m/s, an offset of 5 m/s. The integral supplies the 3000 N of resistance with zero error. A 2 % grade adds mg × 0.02 = 1500 × 9.81 × 0.02 = 294 N, which P alone would answer with a further 294 ÷ 600 = 0.49 m/s of error; the integrator absorbs it.

Practical limits: a small λ means a large K<sub>p</sub> and a large force step (5 m/s of error × 500 = 2500 N here), so check the actuator limit; add anti-windup (stop integrating while the force is saturated); filter any derivative; rate-limit the reference or use a reference model 1/(λs + 1) for comfort.
Check: method 2 at t = λ = 3 s reaches 63.2 % of a step (25 to 28.16 m/s for a 5 m/s step), which is what a first-order loop with λ = 3 s must do.

bank.q: An EPS assist map gives motor current against steering torque at three vehicle speeds. Describe how you would calibrate it and how you would add return-to-centre, damping and friction compensation.
outline: Assist current rises with torque but falls with speed; dead band and saturation at the ends
Return-to-centre term from steering angle, active at low speed only
Damping term proportional to steering rate, opposing fast movement
Friction compensation as a small bias that changes sign with steering direction
Blend the terms, then limit current and rate
Test at parking, straight-highway and slalom conditions
answer: Shape of the map: the input is driver torque T<sub>d</sub> from the torsion bar and the vehicle speed; the output is motor current. Below a small dead band (for example ±0.5 N·m) the current is zero, so straight-ahead feel is clean. Above it the current rises with T<sub>d</sub>, steeply at parking and gently at speed, and it stops at a current limit.

answer.text: Example map at a driver torque of 4 N·m (16 : 1 worm, k<sub>t</sub> = 0.05 N·m/A):

answer: Calibration steps: (1) measure the rack force needed at each speed on dry and wet roads; (2) choose the driver torque wanted at each point, light at parking (3 to 5 N·m), heavier and more linear at speed; (3) assist = needed pinion torque − driver torque, converted to current with I = T<sub>assist</sub> ÷ (N k<sub>t</sub>); (4) smooth the table between speeds so the feel does not step.

Return-to-centre: a current proportional to steering angle, I<sub>rtc</sub> = −k<sub>rtc</sub> × θ, acting towards straight ahead. It is faded in at low speed, where the tyres' own self-aligning torque is too weak to bring the wheel back, and faded out at high speed, where it is not needed.

Damping: a current proportional to steering rate, I<sub>damp</sub> = −c × dθ/dt, opposing fast motion. It stops the wheel overshooting the centre when the driver lets go, and calms kickback on rough roads. It needs the angle sensor signal and a filter on the rate.

Friction compensation: a small fixed current in the direction the wheel is turning, I<sub>f</sub> = I<sub>0</sub> × sign(dθ/dt), with a smooth change near zero rate so it does not chatter. It cancels the friction of the column, worm and rack so the steering feels light and the same in both directions.

Blending and limits: total current = map current + return-to-centre + damping + friction compensation; then limit the current (for example 60 to 80 A), its rate of change, and the motor temperature, with a thermal model that reduces assist at a long full-lock hold.

Tests: parking (lock-to-lock at standstill: effort and current peak), straight highway (on-centre feel, return and stability with hands off for a moment), and slalom or step steer (damping, no overshoot, no lag between driver torque and assist). Repeat on low-grip surfaces and at hot and cold temperatures.
Check: each current in the table is assist ÷ (16 × 0.05) = assist ÷ 0.8, so 40, 12 and 4 N·m give 50, 15 and 5 A.

bank.q: For a quarter-car model of one corner, write the equations of body and wheel motion and explain how a skyhook controller computes the actuator force.
outline: Two masses: sprung m<sub>s</sub> and unsprung m<sub>u</sub>, spring k<sub>s</sub>, tyre stiffness k<sub>t</sub>, damper c<sub>s</sub>
Equations from Newton's second law for each mass, with actuator force F<sub>a</sub> in between
Skyhook target: force that damps body velocity against the sky
Force = −c<sub>sky</sub> × body velocity, clipped to the actuator's limits
Trade-off between body flatness and wheel grip; need for a force limit
answer: Model: sprung (body) mass m<sub>s</sub> on a spring k<sub>s</sub>, a damper c<sub>s</sub> and an actuator force F<sub>a</sub>, above the unsprung (wheel) mass m<sub>u</sub>, which sits on the tyre stiffness k<sub>t</sub> over the road height z<sub>r</sub>. Displacements z<sub>s</sub> and z<sub>u</sub> are measured upward from rest.

answer.text: Equations (Newton's second law for each mass; F<sub>a</sub> pushes the body up and the wheel down):
answer.pre:
m<sub>s</sub> z̈<sub>s</sub> = −k<sub>s</sub> (z<sub>s</sub> − z<sub>u</sub>) − c<sub>s</sub> (ż<sub>s</sub> − ż<sub>u</sub>) + F<sub>a</sub>
m<sub>u</sub> z̈<sub>u</sub> =  k<sub>s</sub> (z<sub>s</sub> − z<sub>u</sub>) + c<sub>s</sub> (ż<sub>s</sub> − ż<sub>u</sub>) − k<sub>t</sub> (z<sub>u</sub> − z<sub>r</sub>) − F<sub>a</sub>

answer: Typical numbers: m<sub>s</sub> = 400 kg, m<sub>u</sub> = 40 kg, k<sub>s</sub> = 20 kN/m, k<sub>t</sub> = 200 kN/m. Body frequency ≈ √(k<sub>s</sub>/m<sub>s</sub>) ÷ 2π = √50 ÷ 6.283 = 1.13 Hz; wheel-hop frequency ≈ √((k<sub>s</sub> + k<sub>t</sub>)/m<sub>u</sub>) ÷ 2π = √5500 ÷ 6.283 = 11.8 Hz. The controller must handle both.

Skyhook target: imagine a damper from the body to a fixed point in the sky. Its force F<sub>a</sub> = −c<sub>sky</sub> ż<sub>s</sub> opposes body velocity only, not wheel velocity, so it calms the body without stiffening the wheel. Body velocity comes from integrating the corner accelerometer, with a high-pass filter to stop drift.
How much damping: c<sub>sky</sub> = 5000 N·s/m on this corner gives a body damping ratio ζ = c<sub>sky</sub> ÷ (2√(k<sub>s</sub>m<sub>s</sub>)) = 5000 ÷ (2 × 2828) = 0.88, a well-damped body.

Computing the force: at ż<sub>s</sub> = +0.08 m/s the target is −5000 × 0.08 = −400 N. A fully active electromagnetic actuator of 250 N/A needs 1.6 A. A semi-active damper can give it only when F × v<sub>rel</sub> < 0, with v<sub>rel</sub> = ż<sub>s</sub> − ż<sub>u</sub>: if the wheel moves down at 0.12 m/s, v<sub>rel</sub> = 0.20 m/s and c = 400 ÷ 0.20 = 2000 N·s/m; if the wheel moves up at 0.18 m/s, v<sub>rel</sub> = −0.10 m/s, the force cannot be made and the damper goes to minimum.
Clipping: the command is limited to the actuator's force (or, for a damper, its c<sub>min</sub> to c<sub>max</sub>), and to its rate and bandwidth.

Trade-off: pure skyhook leaves the wheel almost undamped, so near 11.8 Hz the tyre load varies more and grip falls. Practical controllers add some damping on the wheel (groundhook) or blend in passive damping, and limit the force so the wheel stays on the road.
Check: the skyhook force has the opposite sign to body velocity (−400 N for +0.08 m/s), and the semi-active case 1 satisfies F × v<sub>rel</sub> = −80 < 0.

bank.q: Describe the sensor set of an ADAS and trace, block by block, how one radar measurement becomes a brake request.
outline: Sensors: radar, camera, ultrasonic, lidar where fitted, plus vehicle speed and yaw rate
Perception: detect and track objects, give range, range rate, angle
Fusion: match radar and camera tracks with time alignment and Kalman filtering
Planning: pick the target, compute TTC and required deceleration
Actuation: brake request to ESP, torque request to the powertrain, warning to the driver
Levels of automation and the hand-back to the driver

head: Sensor
Gives
Strong in
Weak in
rows: distance up to a few metres

answer: Radar measurement: the radar sends a frequency-modulated wave and compares the echo. The delay gives range, the Doppler shift gives range rate (closing speed), and the antenna array gives angle. Each scan returns a list of detections.

Perception: detections are grouped into objects and tracked from scan to scan; each track gets range, range rate, angle and a confidence. Stationary echoes from bridges and signs are separated from a real stopped car using height, size and the camera.

Fusion: radar and camera tracks are time-aligned (each has a time stamp), moved into one vehicle coordinate frame and matched; a Kalman filter combines them into one object with position, speed and type. The fused object is more certain than either sensor alone.

Planning: the target is the nearest object in the predicted path of the host (from yaw rate and steering angle). For a stopped car at 25 m with the host at 13.9 m/s, TTC = 25 ÷ 13.9 = 1.80 s. The deceleration needed after the 0.5 s system delay is 13.9² ÷ (2 × (25 − 6.95)) = 193.2 ÷ 36.1 = 5.35 m/s², within the 8 m/s² the brakes can give, so a full stop is still possible.

Actuation: first a warning to the driver (sound, lamp), then a pre-fill of the brakes, then a brake request over CAN to the ESP unit, which builds the pressure; a torque-cut request goes to the powertrain. The brakes then follow s = vt<sub>d</sub> + v²/(2a) = 6.95 + 12.08 = 19.03 m, which leaves 5.97 m of margin at 25 m.

Levels of automation: AEB and adaptive cruise are SAE Level 1 functions; with lane keeping together they make Level 2, where the driver must still monitor and take over at any time. When a sensor is blocked or the situation is outside the design, the system warns and hands back.
Check: from 18 m the same chain needs 19.03 m, so it cannot stop; it still cuts the impact speed to 4.05 m/s, which is why AEB is described as reducing impact speed at higher speeds.

bank.q: Compare ABS, traction control and ESP: which sensors each needs, which actuators each uses, and why all three share one hydraulic unit and one controller.
outline: ABS: four wheel speeds, inlet and outlet valves, pump; brake only
TCS: same wheel speeds plus engine torque control and, if needed, brake at the spinning wheel
ESP: adds steering angle, yaw rate and lateral acceleration; brakes one wheel at a time
Shared hardware reduces cost, weight and wiring; requirements on valve speed and pressure estimation
Failure modes: one sensor out, degraded modes, warning lamp
Why the split into three functions is software, not hardware

head: ABS
Traction control (TCS)
ESP
rows: brake slip, λ near the peak
wheel speeds, steering angle, yaw rate, lateral acceleration, brake pressure
inlet and outlet valves, return pump
engine torque (throttle, spark, fuel) and the spinning wheel's brake
brake at any one wheel (needs a pump that builds pressure without the pedal), engine torque

answer: ABS: reduces brake pressure at a wheel that is heading for lock, so λ stays near the friction peak (for example releasing at λ = 0.40, holding at 0.145, building at 0.055 with v = 20 m/s and r = 0.30 m). It can only lower the pressure the driver makes.

TCS: uses the same wheel speeds to find a driven wheel spinning faster than the car (λ negative, for example −0.8 at ωr = 36 m/s and v = 20 m/s). It cuts engine torque and brakes the spinning wheel; with an open differential the brake on the spinning wheel lets the other wheel carry more torque.

ESP: adds the steering angle, yaw rate and lateral acceleration sensors, builds a reference yaw rate r<sub>des</sub> = vδ ÷ (L + Kv²) and brakes one wheel to correct the error, for example 1500 N·m of yaw moment from 2000 N at the rear inner wheel of a 1.5 m track. It must build brake pressure with the driver's foot off the pedal, so its unit has extra switching valves and a self-priming pump.

Why one hydraulic unit: all three need fast, separate pressure control at each wheel; ESP's unit already contains ABS's inlet and outlet valves and pump. Sharing saves cost, weight, piping and wiring, and the functions must not fight: one controller sets priorities (ABS slip limits stay active while ESP brakes a wheel).

Why one controller: the same wheel speed signals and the same vehicle speed estimate are used by all three, and a single ECU avoids time delays and disagreements between boxes. The split into ABS, TCS and ESP is a split in software functions running on one ECU, not in hardware.

Demands on the shared unit: valves that switch in a few milliseconds, a pump that can build pressure quickly, and good pressure estimation (a pressure sensor at the master cylinder plus valve models), because ESP needs a known brake force at one wheel.

Failure modes: if one wheel speed sensor fails, ABS, TCS and ESP lose that wheel; the ECU switches them off (or to a reduced mode), lights the warning lamps and leaves normal braking working. If the yaw sensor fails, ESP is switched off but ABS can stay on. EBD (rear brake force limiting) is kept as long as possible.

Check: each function adds sensors to the one before it (ABS → TCS adds engine control, ESP adds three chassis sensors), and the actuator list grows the same way, which is why they are built as one unit.

bank.q: A car with ACC, ESP and electric power steering must share wheel speeds, steering angle and yaw rate. Analyse how one sensor set can serve all three, and what happens when one sensor fails.
outline: Wheel speed sensors serve ABS, TCS, ESP and speed for ACC and EPS
Steering angle sensor serves ESP reference yaw rate and EPS return-to-centre
Yaw rate and lateral acceleration serve ESP and ACC curve handling
Plausibility checks against each other; CAN message sharing and time stamps
Failure: fallback values, degraded function, tell-tale lamp, driver warning
Safety argument: never silently keep full function on a failed sensor
answer: One sensor set, many users: each sensor is read by its owner (wheel speeds and yaw rate by the ESP unit, steering angle by EPS or the column module) and broadcast on CAN with a time stamp and a status bit; ACC, ESP and EPS read the same messages, so they see the same numbers at the same time.

Plausibility checks against each other: for a car at 20 m/s, a yaw rate of 0.20 rad/s means a lateral acceleration v × r = 4 m/s², and a difference between the outer and inner wheel speeds of r × track = 0.20 × 1.5 = 0.30 m/s. The bicycle model gives a third estimate from the steering angle. If one signal disagrees with the other two beyond a tolerance, that signal is marked faulty.

Failure of a wheel speed sensor: ESP and ABS switch off or go to a reduced mode; ACC switches off (it needs a trusted host speed and brake authority); EPS uses a fallback speed (from the other wheels or a fixed medium value) so the assist neither goes too light at speed nor too heavy at parking.

Failure of the steering angle sensor: ESP loses its reference and switches off; EPS loses return-to-centre and damping but keeps the torque-based assist; ACC loses lane prediction and may switch off or keep only straight-road following.
Failure of the yaw rate sensor: ESP switches off; ACC can estimate path curvature from the wheel speed difference and steering angle for a while, with reduced performance; EPS is unaffected.

Safety argument: a function never keeps full authority on a failed sensor without saying so. Each degraded mode lights a tell-tale lamp and shows a message, the driver is told which function is lost, and the remaining functions are those whose inputs are still trusted.

Check: the three independent yaw estimates in the plausibility step agree (0.20 rad/s from the gyro, 4 m/s² ÷ 20 m/s = 0.20 rad/s, 0.30 m/s ÷ 1.5 m = 0.20 rad/s), which is what lets the ECU single out a faulty one.

bank.q: Evaluate the design choices in an airbag system: where the crash sensors sit, how the firing threshold is set, how fast the bag must inflate, and why the seat belt must still be worn.
outline: Sensors: front accelerometers, side pressure or acceleration sensors, rollover sensing
Threshold: severe enough deceleration within a short window, with a safing sensor to prevent false fire
Timing: full inflation in tens of milliseconds, before the occupant moves far
Bag vents energy, belt carries the steady restraint; unbelted occupant needs different tuning
Hazards: out-of-position occupants, child seats, bag replacement after firing
answer: Where the sensors sit: the main accelerometer is in the airbag ECU near the centre of the car, where it feels the whole crash pulse; front upfront sensors in the crush zone see a severe frontal crash early; side sensors (accelerometers in the pillars or pressure sensors in the doors) are needed because a side impact gives only a few milliseconds; a roll-rate sensor with lateral accelerometers detects rollover. Evaluation: central plus satellite sensors give both early and reliable detection.

How the threshold is set: the ECU filters the acceleration, integrates it to a speed change Δv and fires only when Δv and its rate cross a stored curve for a few milliseconds, with an independent safing sensor agreeing. Frontal thresholds are roughly a speed change of 15 to 25 km/h. Evaluation: too low a threshold fires on kerb strikes and parking knocks; too high misses real crashes; the safing sensor guards against a single fault.

How fast the bag must inflate: for a 50 km/h barrier crash with 0.6 m of crush, a = 13.9² ÷ (2 × 0.6) = 161 m/s² (16.4 g) and the car stops in 2 × 0.6 ÷ 13.9 = 86 ms. The bag must be full before the head of the belted occupant reaches it; with the threshold crossed near 10 ms, firing near 25 ms and about 25 ms to fill, it is full near 50 ms, well inside the pulse. Side bags have only 5 to 10 ms.

Venting: the bag vents through holes and fabric so it softens as the occupant arrives; it spreads the load over the head and chest, while the belt with pretensioner and load limiter carries the main restraint force through the pelvis and rib cage.

Why the belt must still be worn: SRS means supplemental. An unbelted occupant moves early and far and can meet the bag while it is still opening at high speed; the belt also keeps the occupant in place in side impacts, rollovers and second impacts where the frontal bag does not help.

Hazards and their design answers: out-of-position occupants (seat sensors, two-stage inflators, depowered bags); rear-facing child seats (passenger occupant detection and bag suppression); a fired module must be replaced, and the ECU stores the crash record and must usually be replaced too.

Overall evaluation: the design trades early firing (needs sensors near the impact and low thresholds) against false firing (needs safing and held thresholds); the numbers above show the bag must work inside the 86 ms crash pulse, which only a belted occupant matches well.
Check: t = 2s ÷ v = 1.2 ÷ 13.9 = 0.086 s agrees with v ÷ a = 13.9 ÷ 161; a bag full at 50 ms is well inside it.

bank.q: Evaluate PI versus PD control for vehicle speed. Explain why practical speed loops use PI and where the damping that PD would give is obtained instead.
outline: PD acts on the error's rate; in speed loops it amplifies sensor noise and can fight the throttle's own lag
PI gives zero steady-state error against grade and headwind, which matters more than extra damping
Damping comes from the plant's inertia and from rate limits and feed-forward on the throttle map
Where PD does appear: inner torque loops and active suspension damping
Practical gain limits, anti-windup and override by the driver
answer: Plant: m dv/dt = F − bv; for m = 1500 kg, b = 100 N/(m/s) the speed loop sees a first-order lag with τ = 15 s. The controller must hold speed against resistance, grade and wind, and follow a new set speed comfortably.

PD law: F = K<sub>p</sub>e + K<sub>d</sub> de/dt. At steady state de/dt = 0, so PD is the same as P: the speed settles where K<sub>p</sub>e = bv. With K<sub>p</sub> = 500 and v<sub>ref</sub> = 30 m/s, v = 25 m/s and e = 5 m/s, and every 2 % of grade (294 N) adds 294 ÷ 600 = 0.49 m/s more. A driver notices a 5 m/s (18 km/h) offset at once.

PI law: F = K<sub>p</sub>e + K<sub>i</sub>∫e dt. The integral keeps growing while any error remains, so at steady state e = 0 against any constant resistance, grade or wind; this is the main requirement of cruise control.

Noise: the wheel speed signal has noise from tooth spacing and road roughness. With a 10 ms sample, noise of 0.05 m/s between samples looks like 0.05 ÷ 0.01 = 5 m/s² of acceleration; with K<sub>d</sub> = 200 N/(m/s²) that is 1000 N of chattering force, the same size as the force the loop needs. A filter s/(T<sub>f</sub>s + 1) helps but adds lag.

Lag: the throttle and engine respond with their own delay; derivative action pushes hard on the first sign of change and can fight that delay, giving a jerky response. The speed loop does not need it, because the plant is first order and has no oscillation of its own to damp.

Where the damping comes from instead: the car's inertia and resistance (τ = 15 s) already make the loop well damped; lambda tuning (T<sub>i</sub> = τ) gives a first-order, non-overshooting response; a reference model 1/(λs + 1) or a rate limit on v<sub>ref</sub> smooths the force demand (no 2500 N jump for a 5 m/s step); and feed-forward from the throttle map and road grade gives fast response without high gain.

Where PD does appear: in inner loops with oscillating dynamics, such as a torque loop with driveline shuffle, an electronic throttle position loop, or active suspension damping, where the derivative term is the damping force itself.
Practical points for the PI: anti-windup when the throttle is fully open or closed; gain limits so the force step stays inside the actuator; and override by the driver on the brake or accelerator.

head: PD
PI
rows: Steady error on a level road

answer: Verdict: PI is used for vehicle speed because zero steady error matters more than extra damping, and the damping PD would add is not needed and costs noise. Check: P or PD with K<sub>p</sub> = 500 leaves e = bv<sub>ref</sub> ÷ (K<sub>p</sub> + b) = 3000 ÷ 600 = 5 m/s; PI leaves 0.

glossary.def: The fractional difference between vehicle speed and wheel rim speed, λ = (v − ωr)/v, which sets how much grip a tyre gives.
The speed at which the car turns about its vertical axis, measured by a yaw rate sensor in degrees per second.
The turning moment about the vertical axis made by a single wheel's brake force acting at a distance from the centre of gravity.
The condition where the car turns less than the steering asks for, so the front wheels run wide.
The condition where the car turns more than the steering asks for, so the rear swings out.
The gap to the vehicle ahead divided by your speed, in seconds (also called the time gap); ACC controls this rather than distance.
The gap divided by the closing speed, in seconds; a measure used to warn or brake before a rear-end hit.
The stored set of upshift and downshift speeds against throttle opening that fixes when the gearbox changes gear.
A calibrated bar that twists in proportion to the torque applied through it, used in EPS to measure steering torque.
The lookup table that turns measured steering torque and vehicle speed into a motor current for power steering.
An EPS function that steers the wheels back towards straight ahead at low speed when the driver lets go.
A control term that adds a small torque in the direction of motion to overcome stiction in the steering or pedal mechanism.
A suspension control law that damps the body against a notional fixed reference while leaving the wheels free.
A two-mass model of one corner of a car, with the sprung body mass on a spring and damper above the unsprung wheel mass on the tyre stiffness.
The small electric detonator inside the airbag module that ignites the gas generator on command.
A device that pulls the belt tight within milliseconds of a crash, before the airbag is needed.
The process of merging measurements from several sensors into one consistent description of the surroundings.
The error that remains a long time after a step change when the controller has no integral action to remove it.
The unwanted growth of an integral term while the actuator is saturated, which causes overshoot when the error finally reverses.
A small range of error around the set point inside which the controller deliberately does nothing, to stop actuator chatter.
The shared two-wire serial network over which controllers such as ESP, EPS and the engine ECU exchange signals.
A throttle plate driven by a motor under ECU command, with pedal position as a request rather than a direct link.

Steering whose ratio of road-wheel angle to steering-wheel angle is not fixed: a variable-ratio rack changes it with steering angle, and active steering (a planetary gear and motor in the column) changes it with vehicle speed.
A second, independent crash sensor in series with the airbag firing circuit; the squib fires only when it agrees with the main accelerometer.
The clutch inside a torque converter that ties the turbine to the impeller at cruising speed, removing converter slip; often run with a small controlled slip.
A vehicle model that lumps the two front wheels into one and the two rear wheels into one, used to compute the reference yaw rate.
